title: Neural Bandit with Arm Group Graph

problem.claim: Contextual bandits seek the arm with the highest reward using contextual information.

gap.claim: Existing bandit modeling is presented as insufficiently informed by group behaviors and mutual impacts among arm groups.

contributions.claim: The paper introduces Arm Group Graph, representing arm groups as nodes and inter-group correlations as weighted edges.
The paper proposes AGG-UCB, using neural networks to estimate rewards and graph neural networks to learn correlated arm-group representations.

The paper derives a neural-network-based upper confidence bound and reports a near-optimal regret bound for AGG-UCB with over-parameterized neural networks, together with convergence analysis for GNNs with fully connected layers.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe the Arm Group Graph model and the upper confidence bound as new.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report extensive experiments against state-of-the-art baselines on multiple public datasets.
The authors report that the proposed algorithm is effective based on those experiments.

narrative_sequence.summary: Contextual bandits select high-reward arms from contextual information.
The paper models arm groups and their correlations with Arm Group Graph.
AGG-UCB combines neural reward estimation, GNN representations, and a neural-network-based exploration bound.
The paper reports regret and convergence analyses, followed by experiments on public datasets against baselines.

source_observation.claim: Arm-group correlations are represented explicitly and incorporated into reward learning.

interpretation.claim: Modeling structured relationships among actions may provide useful information for contextual decision-making.

application.claim: When actions exhibit group behavior and inter-group effects, represent those relationships as a graph and integrate them into the decision model.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that graph structure is beneficial when group behaviors or inter-group effects are absent or inaccurately specified.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the datasets, baselines, metrics, or quantitative experimental results.
The abstract does not provide the assumptions or exact form of the regret bound and convergence analysis.
The abstract does not independently verify the authors' reported effectiveness.
